source_text: Οἷος δὲ καὶ ὁ τοῦ Ἡροδότου ἐστὶν Ἄμμων, οὗ τὰς λέξεις ὁ Κέλσος παρείληφεν, ὡς εἰς ἀπόδειξιν περὶ τοῦ δεῖν ἕκαστον τὰ πάτρια τηρεῖν; ὁ γὰρ Ἄμμων αὐτῶν τοῖς τῶν ἀπὸ Μαρέης πόλεως καὶ Ἄπιος οἰκοῦσι τὰ πρόσουρα τῇ Λιβύῃ οὐκ ἐᾷ ἀδιαφορεῖν πρὸς τὴν χρῆσιν τῶν θηλέων βοῶν· ὅπερ πρᾶγμα οὐ μόνον τῇ φύσει ἑαυτοῦ ἀδιάφορόν ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ οὐ κωλύει καλὸν καὶ ἀγαθὸν εἶναί τινα. καὶ εἰ μὲν ὁ Ἄμμων αὐτῶν ἀπηγόρευε τὴν χρῆσιν τῶν θηλειῶν βοῶν διὰ τὸ εἰς γεωργίαν τοῦ ζῴου χρήσιμον καὶ πρὸς τούτῳ διὰ τὸ διὰ τῶν θηλέων μάλιστα αὔξειν τὸ γένος αὐτῶν, τάχα ἂν εἶχε πιθανότητα ὁ λόγος· νυνὶ δὲ ἅπαξ βούλεται αὐτοὺς ἐμπίνοντας τοῦ Νείλου δεῖν τηρεῖν τοὺς Αἰγυπτίων περὶ θηλειῶν βοῶν νόμους. καὶ ἐπὶ τούτῳ γε τωθάζων ὁ Κέλσος τοὺς παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις ἀγγέλους πρεσβεύοντας τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ οὐ κακίονα ἔφησεν εἶναι τὸν Ἄμμωνα πρὸς τὸ διαπρεσβεῦσαι τὰ δαιμόνια ἢ οἱ Ἰουδαίων ἄγγελοι· ὧν οὐκ ἐξήτασε τοὺς λόγους καὶ τὰς ἐπιφανείας, τί βούλονται. ἑωράκει γὰρ ἂν ὅτι οὐ „τῶν βοῶν μέλει τῷ θεῷ,“ ἔνθα καὶ δοκεῖ περὶ βοῶν ἢ ἀλόγων ζῴων νομοθετεῖν, ἀλλὰ τὰ δι᾿ ἀνθρώπους γραφέντα ἐν προσχήματι τῷ περὶ ἀλόγων ζῴων φυσιολογίαν τινὰ περιέχει. Κέλσος μὲν οὖν οὐδὲν ἄδικόν φησι ποιεῖν ἕκαστον, τὰ σφέτερα νόμιμα θρησκεύειν ἐθέλοντα· καὶ ἀκολουθεῖ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν μηδὲν ἄδικον ποιεῖν Σκύθας, ἐπεὶ κατὰ τὰ πάτρια δαίνυνται ἀνθρώπους. καὶ Ἰνδῶν δὲ οἱ τοὺς πατέρας ἐσθίοντες ὅσια δρᾶν νομίζουσι, καὶ κατὰ τὸν Κέλσον, ἢ οὐκ ἄδικά γε. ἐκτίθεται γοῦν Ἡροδότου λέξιν συναγορεύουσαν τὸ ἕκαστον τοῖς πατρίοις νόμοις καθηκόντως χρῆσθαι, καὶ ἔοικεν ἀποδεχομένῳ τοὺς ἐπὶ Δαρείου Καλατίας καλουμένους Ἰνδοὺς τοὺς γονεῖς κατεσθίοντας, ἐπεὶ πρὸς τὸν Δαρεῖον πυνθανόμενον, ἐπὶ πόσῳ χρήματι ἀποθέσθαι τοῦτον τὸν νόμον βούλονται, ἀναβοήσαντες μέγα εὐφημεῖν αὐτὸν ἐκέλευον.
thought_title: Herodotus’s Ammon and the customs of Scythians and Indians
pass_a_gloss: Of what sort (οἷος) is also the Ammon of Herodotus, whose words (λέξεις) Celsus has taken over (παρείληφεν) as for proof (ἀπόδειξις) about each needing to keep (τηρεῖν) ancestral things? For their Ammon does not allow (ἐᾷ) those from the city of Marea and Apis, inhabiting the parts bordering Libya, to be indifferent (ἀδιαφορεῖν) toward the use (χρῆσις) of female cattle; which matter (πρᾶγμα) is not only indifferent (ἀδιάφορον) by its own nature (φύσις), but also does not hinder (κωλύει) someone being noble and good (καλὸν καὶ ἀγαθόν). And if their Ammon forbade (ἀπηγόρευε) the use of female cattle because of the animal (ζῷον) being useful (χρήσιμον) for farming (γεωργία) and besides because the stock (γένος) increases (αὔξειν) most through the females, perhaps the word/argument (λόγος) would have had plausibility (πιθανότης); but now (νυνί) he once for all/simply (ἅπαξ) wants them, drinking of the Nile, to have to keep the Egyptians' laws (νόμους) about female cattle. And mocking (τωθάζων) at this point the angels among the Jews acting as envoys of (πρεσβεύοντας) the things of God, Celsus said that Ammon was not worse at conveying the divine things than the angels of the Jews; whose words (λόγοι) and appearances (ἐπιφάνειαι) he did not examine (ἐξήτασε), what they mean (τί βούλονται). For he would have seen that God does not care (μέλει) for oxen (βόες), even where he seems to legislate (νομοθετεῖν) about oxen or irrational animals (ἄλογα ζῷα), but the things written for the sake of men (δι᾿ ἀνθρώπους γραφέντα) under a pretext/outward form (πρόσχημα) about irrational animals contain a certain account of nature (φυσιολογία). Celsus then says each does nothing unjust (ἄδικον) wishing to practise (θρησκεύειν) his own customs (νόμιμα); and it follows according to him that Scythians do nothing unjust, since according to ancestral things they feast on (δαίνυνται) men. And of Indians those eating their fathers think they do holy things (ὅσια δρᾶν), and according to Celsus [they do], or at least not unjust things. He sets out, then (γοῦν), a passage of Herodotus pleading (συναγορεύουσαν) for each fittingly (καθηκόντως) using ancestral laws, and he seems like one approving (ἀποδεχομένῳ) the Indians in Darius's time called Callatiae, devouring (κατεσθίοντας) their parents, since to Darius inquiring (πυνθανόμενον) for how much money they wish to put aside (ἀποθέσθαι) this law, crying out loudly (ἀναβοήσαντες μέγα) they bade him keep holy silence (εὐφημεῖν).

pass_b_english: And what, too, is Herodotus’s Ammon like, whose words Celsus has taken over as if to prove that each people must keep its ancestral customs? For their Ammon does not allow the people from the city of Marea and from Apis, who live in the parts bordering on Libya, to treat the use of cows as indifferent; and yet this is a thing that is not only indifferent by its own nature, but also does not prevent anyone from being noble and good. If their Ammon had forbidden the use of cows because the animal is useful for farming, and besides because the stock increases mostly through the females, his word might perhaps have had some plausibility. But as it is, he simply insists that because they drink of the Nile they must keep the Egyptians’ laws about cows.

And it was on this point that Celsus, mocking the angels among the Jews who serve as envoys of the things of God, said that Ammon was no worse an envoy of divine things than the angels of the Jews. Yet he did not examine their words and their appearances, to see what they mean. For he would have seen that “God does not care for oxen” (1 Corinthians 9:9), even where He seems to be making laws about oxen or animals without reason (Deuteronomy 25:4), but that what was written for the sake of human beings (1 Corinthians 9:10), under the outward appearance of dealing with animals without reason, contains a teaching about the nature of things.

Celsus, then, says that each people does nothing wrong in wishing to practise its own customs. On his view it follows that the Scythians do nothing wrong, since they feast on men according to their ancestral customs. And those Indians who eat their fathers think they do a holy thing, and according to Celsus they do so, or at least do nothing wrong. At any rate he sets out a passage of Herodotus that argues that each people does right to follow its ancestral laws, and he seems to approve of the Indians of Darius’s time called Callatiae, who eat their parents, since, when Darius asked them for what sum they would be willing to give up this law, they cried out loudly and told him to speak no words of ill omen.
notes: οὐ τῶν βοῶν μέλει τῷ θεῷ is Paul's question in 1 Corinthians 9:9 (μὴ τῶν βοῶν μέλει τῷ θεῷ;) turned into a statement; 'the law about oxen' it comments on is Deuteronomy 25:4 ('You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain'), cited at the clause 'making laws about oxen'. δι᾿ ἀνθρώπους γραφέντα echoes 1 Corinthians 9:10 (δι᾿ ἡμᾶς γὰρ ἐγράφη). φυσιολογίαν τινά: literally 'a certain natural philosophy / account of nature'; Origen means a deeper meaning about the nature of things (human and spiritual), rendered 'a teaching about the nature of things'. ὁ λόγος in 'his word might have had plausibility' could mean 'the argument' (Celsus's) or Ammon's 'pronouncement'; context (Ammon forbade) favours Ammon's word. ἅπαξ: 'simply, once for all'. καὶ κατὰ τὸν Κέλσον, ἢ οὐκ ἄδικά γε: elliptical; 'they do holy things' is understood. Origen paraphrases Darius's question as 'give up this law' (ἀποθέσθαι τοῦτον τὸν νόμον), which differs from Herodotus's wording (burn their fathers); the translation keeps Origen's wording. τοὺς παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις ἀγγέλους πρεσβεύοντας τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ: 'angels who serve as envoys of the things of God' (parallel to Celsus's 'envoy of divine things'); 'God' capitalised as Origen's own term for the true God.
Open doubt (review): 5.36: in 'his word might perhaps have had some plausibility', ὁ λόγος could mean Ammon's ruling or the argument. The reading as Ammon's ruling is kept.
